newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo study calls for plan to address surplus labour.
newsitem.headline: Yugo study calls for plan to address surplus labour.

text.p: Yugoslavia must have a clear social programme to resolve the problem of surplus labour which planned reforms will only aggravate, the Belgrade-based Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) said in its latest study.
"In industry alone, we now have a surplus of some 570,000 workers, or 67 percent," IEN economist Milena Jovicic said.
Official statistics registered around 2.02 million employed in Yugoslavia in February, 827,000 of them in industry and mining. The data does not cover the private sector.
There are no official figures for unemployment, but independent economists said it was around 25 percent, while many workers in idle factories are on paid "compulsory leave".

Nearly four years of war-related international sanctions have crippled the economy, with industrial capacities running at barely over 30 percent of their level in 1990, the year before the former Yugoslav federation broke up.
The degree of capacity utilisation, pace of industrial growth, declining exports and other negative economic trends do not indicate any improvement in the near future, Jovicic said.

Surplus labour is most pronounced in metal processing, machine building, electrical and chemical industries, with the largest number of workers, but the situation in trade, tourism, catering and transport sectors is similar, the institute said.
"The announced Privatisation Law must be viewed in the light of resolving these problems as well," Jovicic said.

Serbia last month unveiled a draft privatisation law that has been criticised by economists and some trade unions for not being accompanied by a new social policy to deal with the growing unemployment its implementation was bound to bring.
Reforms must be carried out and viewed comprehensively, and not as the isolated settlement of individual problems, said Jovicic.
"The problem of surplus labour is very painful in Yugoslavia," said Aleksandra Posarac, another IEN economist.

According to the institute, official economic policy appeared to be waiting for an increase in output under the existing industrial structure, which would automatically result in less surplus workers.
"Analyses have shown it is practically impossible to expect substantial increase in output and employment with the existing structure of industry," Posarac said.
Structural adjustment is absolutely necessary and it is inevitably accompanied by lay-offs.
"But that should not happen overnight. It is a complex process which cannot stand isolated because it creates huge problems," Posarac said.

The institute said the process should be in stages and take three to five years, with the government providing compensation to laid off workers and an active employment policy which would include retraining.
Surplus labour could be absorbed through the development of the private sector, above all small and medium sized firms, as experience in transition economies has shown, it said.
Stubborn insistence on maintaining large unprofitable systems means sooner or later most of their workers will be out of their jobs, the institute said.

"If there is no clear social programme, the agony of the Yugoslav economy will only be deepened and prolonged. The burden of reforms should be distributed more equally and not just fall on workers," Posarac said. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
